Eggs of the Greater thornbird, incubated under controlled conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], typically hatch after 17 days [ab = 17 days]. This incubation period is notably brief for a furnariid of this body size, reflecting the species’ strategy of rapid embryonic development within a relatively small, thinly walled nest cavity. Field measurements indicate newly hatched nestlings have a wet weight at birth of approximately 11.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 11.5 grams], a value derived from extrapolated growth-curve data rather than direct weighing of neonates at the moment of hatching. This initial mass is modest, representing just under one-third of the asymptotic nestling body mass, which is reached after several weeks of intensive parental provisioning. The altricial condition of the chicks is evident in their sparse down, closed eyes, and complete dependence on brooding and feeding by both adults during the first week post-hatching. Rapid mass gain is fueled by frequent deliveries of arthropod prey, with the nestlings doubling their birth weight within the first four days of exogenous feeding.

Under typical thermal conditions recorded in the species’ active metabolic range of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], post-hatching development proceeds along a well-defined schedule. Nestlings achieve fledging at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a developmental milestone marked by the attainment of sustained flight and departure from the bulky stick nest at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early fledging age is relatively short compared to other sympatric furnariids, allowing the brooding adults to initiate a subsequent nesting attempt within the same breeding season. The chicks, though independent in terms of locomotion, continue to receive supplemental feedings from the parents for another week or so as they refine their foraging skills on surrounding thorn scrub. This brief post-fledging dependency period is characteristic of many suboscine passerines that inhabit unpredictable, semiarid environments where rapid reproductive turnover may confer a selective advantage. The brevity of the nestling phase thus represents a critical window for mass accumulation and feather development necessary for viable flight.

Sexual maturation in the Greater thornbird occurs at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching], a remarkably rapid progression to puberty for a Neotropical passerine of its body size at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. At this stage, maintained under the elevated body temperature typical of active thermoregulation at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the young birds exhibit full adult plumage, gonadal recrudescence, and the onset of territorial singing. Individuals generally do not breed immediately upon reaching puberty; instead, the first successful reproductive event is deferred until approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay likely reflects the need for young birds to acquire and defend a suitable nesting territory, as well as to accumulate sufficient foraging experience to sustain the energetic demands of egg production and chick provisioning. The divergence between the attainment of physiological maturity and actual first breeding is a common life-history pattern among sedentary tropical passerines, where competition for high-quality nesting sites can be intense. The deferred onset of reproduction thus represents a combination of extended behavioral maturation and ecological constraints.

Reproductive output is constrained by both clutch size and the frequency of nesting attempts that are viable within a single year. Females typically lay between three and five eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between three and five eggs per clutch], with four being the most frequently observed number across multiple field studies in the Brazilian Cerrado and Pantanal. The clutch size shows only modest variation, which is consistent with the species’ reliance on a single annual brood under most climatic conditions; indeed, the typical reproductive schedule often results in just one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. Under conditions sustained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], this yields a maximum annual reproductive rate that reflects the trade-off between current investment and residual reproductive value. The large, elaborately structured nest—a conspicuous thorny stick construction suspended between branches—represents a significant parental investment in both construction time and predation risk. The combination of moderately sized clutches and infrequent nesting episodes suggests that adult survival and nest-site persistence are strong selective forces shaping this species’ life history.

Maximum longevity recorded for the Greater thornbird in the wild, under the thermal regime typical of its active metabolic state at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], is approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years]. This extended lifespan is notable among suboscine passerines and is consistent with life-history theory predictions for a species exhibiting low annual reproductive output and high nest-site fidelity. The asymptotic body mass of adult birds reaches about 37 grams [Wwi = about 37 grams], placing this species at the upper end of the mass range for its genus Phacellodomus. The adult body mass is attained after a sustained growth phase that spans several months beyond the fledging period. Combining this relatively large adult size with a low reproductive rate and considerable potential longevity, the Greater thornbird exemplifies a slow-paced life history among Neotropical passerines, likely an adaptation to the region’s pronounced seasonality and the high costs associated with constructing and maintaining its massive arboreal nests over multiple breeding attempts.
